The test section had a 3-leg serpentine channel with a square cross-section of 6.67 x 6.67 cm in the first two legs, and 6.67 x 3.3 cm in the third leg.
Rounded trip strips were attached to the lower surface, spaced 5.08 cm apart and oriented 90 degrees to the airflow.
The rib height-to-channel height ratio was 0.076 and the rib pitch-to-height ratio was 10.
Eight 0.38 cm diameter bleed holes were drilled into the lower surface of the first leg, spaced 5.08 cm apart.
Heat transfer measurements were obtained using a transient liquid crystal technique.
Four bleed flow conditions were tested: no bleed, uniform bleed, increasing bleed, and decreasing bleed.
The bleed flow rates ranged from 5-10% of the total inlet mass flow.
Placing the ribs near the bleed holes (0.51 cm upstream) resulted in greater heat transfer enhancement compared to ribs placed between the bleed holes.
Higher bleed flow rates yielded higher heat transfer values near and away from the bleed holes.
Increasing the Reynolds number from 31,000 to 96,000 decreased the Nusselt number ratio slightly.
The highest heat transfer occurred on the top surface of the rib and downstream of the bleed hole.
Static pressure changed little through the first passage and first turn, then began to decrease halfway down the second passage.
The average cross-sectional air temperatures remained fairly constant along the first passage, with a noticeable increase between the first and second passages.
Spanwise temperature variations were generally greater than streamwise variations.
The uncertainty in the heat transfer coefficients ranged from 8 to 13 percent.
